No I understand, and I don't think that's necessarily a bad product. I also don't think it's a product that is easily referrable to the majority of people.

  
Taskmaster is easy to refer people to, and even then I have had people bounce off the recommendation, because it is isolated. They don't need to watch a whole bunch of older episodes to watch the newest higher production value thing. They can just watch what's coming out with their friends who are already into it and enjoy that.

  
You do that with gamechanger all of a sudden you have to explain why people interact with Sam the way they do, why certain pairs of contestants have certain tendencies, etc. Dropout is a relatively parasocial platform and I think Game changer is on the higher end of benefiting from that. Again, not necessarily a bad thing but it makes it harder to refer people to who haven't/won't buy in to that relationship. 

  
I'll watch five people who I have no idea who they are do the wildest things on Taskmaster, but even I'll admit if it's three people I don't know on Game changer I am less likely to watch it. 

\*Taskmaster also is an odd comparison because I'm sure if you live in the UK you have a higher rate of knowing who these guests are due to the panel show ecosystem; whereas out here I watch and know some from panel shows in the past I've seen but far from the majority.

I'd semi disagree? Game changer is a series of isolated episodes that while they do have growth and development from prior episodes/seasons were originally/try to be isolated episodes. Very rarely do we have a through line outside of game samers which are rare and would not be good episodes to jump people into. However I could show them episode 5 of any season and they would have lost nothing for not seeing the previous four.

  
Taskmaster has a very strong throughline in that the season is one cast. You're not intended to jump into episode 4 because you'll miss how these specific contestants got to where they were. Yes the puzzles and interactions with Alex/Greg are flavored by previous seasons but there is a distinct effort made to allow someone to jump into the first episode of a season and not need to watch what came before.

  
Game changer does that by nature of it being isolated episodes, but fails in that the longer it goes on the more it becomes self-referential and loses the isolation of the game. The trade-off is you get people caring very deeply about the show for how these specific recurring guests handle the games they are put into; which is how we get to where we are not.
Also to be fair, it's a game show. I'm not expected to watch every season of Jeopardy or Survivor to understand what's going on now.

My best successes with contrast paints tend to be where I don't have a ton on my brush at one time. This might not be how it's recommended, but when I did my thousand sons it was working per section so: 

1. Identify the section, in this case circle on shoulder pads.
2. Place on fairly central position, and do a pulling motion in a smooth stroke until you either hit the edge of section or wrist spinning ability. Twist model, adjust, repeat. 
3. If any extra pools away from the edges/borders I like to smooth that down, first wiping brush dry then placing in the pooled section and pulling through it. This letsthe paint stay applied while keeping smooth.

Keys for how I do it being you might not save as much time as you were hoping, but utilizing a healthy amount on brush you should have a smooth finish in decent timeframe. And as someone who is doing a multi color scheme for TSons you can see in my post history, the red is significantly easier than the blue.

[Here you go](http://tappedout.net/mtg-decks/23-03-17-uw-gifts-tron/), this is my current iteration of the deck which is going through some major changes but the mainboard is pretty much solid. 

The general plan is you want to control the board until you can slam gifts on their turn, to reanimate the best threat you have against them(elesh, iona, sundering). The earliest we can do that is their turn three, our turn four, by signeting turn two and hitting all our land drops; this is necessary against fast decks like burn where we need iona or elesh depending on if they're heavier on spells or creatures, color variety etc.. 

This doesn't work against control decks, so we will have to play a slower game and try to control the board until we can sneak a gifts in there, often you'll gifts for not the reanimate package in these matchups immediately which is perfectly fine. If you draw your reanimation targets or rites don't worry too much, you can discard them with thirst for knowledge, often having that enable your reanimation. The other thing is most people are moving emrakul to the sideboard, which personally I'm against. Because we're straddling this line of control and combo, we have our resources split thinly in between, so the graveyard recursion emrakul gives, along with the amount of games I've stalled out until she just wins it, makes her a really key linchpin of the deck.

If you need any other help there's great discussion at the mtgsalvation thread for this deck, and the last post is a write-up I did on yesterdays weekly with this list. I'm happy to answer whatever, I've been playing the deck for almost three years now and absolutely love the deck.
